Violent
VY-o-lent
a.
From Latin violentus, forcible, vehement, from vis, force. Webster 1828: forcible; acting with physical strength; moving or acting with vehemence. In Scripture the word is almost always a verdict on a man’s character, and it recoils on the man who earns it.

Biblical Definition

The Psalter’s rule for the violent man is that his violence comes home: His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate (Psalm 7:16). The word pate is the crown of the head, and the image is a stone thrown upward. Proverbs identifies the violent man’s worst work as recruitment rather than assault: A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good (Proverbs 16:29) — he does not merely strike, he persuades. Against these stands the one text where violence is commended, and it is famously difficult: from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force (Matthew 11:12). Whatever else it means, it does not mean the kingdom is seized by human force in the ordinary sense; the surrounding context is John in prison and a generation that would neither dance nor mourn. The old Reformed reading takes it of the earnestness of those who press into the kingdom against every hindrance — men and women who will not be kept out. Isaiah gives the Servant’s contrast in one line: because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth (Isaiah 53:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines VIOLENT as forcible; acting with physical strength or vehemence; moving or acting with impetuosity; produced or effected by force; and, of persons, vehement, passionate, outrageous.

VIOLENT, a. — Forcible; moving or acting with physical strength; urged or driven with force.

Vehement; outrageous; as a violent man; violent passions.

Produced or effected by force; not spontaneous; as a violent death.

Assailant; acting by force; not authorized; as violent measures.

Latin violentus, from vis, force, strength — the root also of violate and violence.

Key Scripture

Psalm 7:16 — "His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate."

Proverbs 16:29 — "A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good."

Matthew 11:12 — "And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force."

Isaiah 53:9 — "And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth."

Modern Corruption

Two opposite errors work on this word: a triumphalist reading of Matthew 11:12 that licenses coercion for the kingdom, and a pacifist reading of Scripture that denies the civil magistrate the sword God gave him.

expand to see more

Matthew 11:12 has been pressed into service by movements that would advance the kingdom by force — the Munster radicals of the sixteenth century, and in another key the modern dominionist rhetoric that speaks of taking territory. The text will not bear it. Christ’s kingdom is not of this world and its weapons are not carnal (John 18:36; 2 Corinthians 10:4), and the Servant of Isaiah 53 is commended precisely for having done no violence. The historic Reformed reading, in Calvin and among the Puritans, is that the phrase describes the vehement earnestness of those pressing into the kingdom despite opposition, not a warrant for coercion. Whoever cites this verse to justify force against neighbours has read past the whole chapter, which ends with the Lord calling the heavy-laden to a yoke that is easy.

The opposite error is equally unbiblical. Romans 13:4 gives the civil magistrate the sword and calls him a minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil; the 1689 Confession affirms that magistracy is lawful and that Christians may serve in it and wage just war. A blanket pacifism that reads the Sermon on the Mount as abolishing the magistrate’s sword confuses the spheres God has distinguished. Personal vengeance is forbidden to the Christian; public justice is committed to the magistrate. Psalm 7:16 is the assurance that binds the two: the believer need not repay the violent man, because his violent dealing will come down upon his own pate whether by the magistrate now or by God at the last.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chamas (H2555), violence, wrong, cruelty; arits (H6184), terrible, oppressive; Greek biazo (G971), to force or press; biastes (G973), a forceful man.

expand to see more

Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence, wrong; the word that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11) and that the Servant had not done (Isaiah 53:9).

Hebrew arits (H6184) — terrible, violent, oppressive; used of the tyrant in Psalms and Isaiah.

Greek biazo (G971) — to force, to press violently; the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence (Matthew 11:12).

Greek biastes (G973) — a forceful or vehement man; the violent take it by force (Matthew 11:12).

Hebrew qodqod (H6936) — the crown of the head, the pate on which the violence descends (Psalm 7:16).

Usage

"His violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate (Psalm 7:16) — the stone thrown upward returns on the thrower."

"A violent man enticeth his neighbour (Proverbs 16:29) — his worst work is recruitment, not assault."

"Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth (Isaiah 53:9) — the Servant’s contrast, and the ground of His innocence."
